claims.text: Pulumi's component state migrations feature lets component authors ship an upgrade path with the component itself.
A Pulumi component state migration translates the saved state of a component and its children before Pulumi works out which resources need to change.
Component state migrations are new in Pulumi (described as 'Pulumi's new component state migrations').
The Pulumi state migrations API is experimental and may change.
A GitHub discussion for component state migrations feedback exists at github.com/pulumi/pulumi/discussions/24799.
A Pulumi docs page exists at /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/components/state-migrations/ (component state migrations guide) that covers the callback contract.
The pulumi/examples repository contains a directory aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration with the AWSX VPC state migration example, containing all three programs (v1, v2, v3) and the migration code.
A Pulumi concepts page on components exists at /docs/iac/concepts/components/.

The example's v1 uses the legacy `awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc` component, creating a VPC with one isolated subnet, a route table and its association, and an internet gateway, with a security group outside the component referring to the VPC.
In AWS, the security group's VPC ID property means that a new VPC would require replacing the security group too (per the AWS CloudFormation EC2 SecurityGroup VpcId documentation).
Without a migration connecting old state to new code, upgrading from the legacy AWSX VPC component to the modern one could replace the VPC instead of keeping it.
If a database is recreated, its replacement does not automatically contain the old data.
The example's second version upgrades to the modern `awsx.ec2.Vpc` component while keeping the existing network.
The example's third version removes AWSX and declares the resources directly with `@pulumi/aws`.
Across all three versions of the example, the AWS resource IDs stay the same and the security group continues to use the same VPC.

In the example, the Pulumi-tracked resource tree in v1 is awsx:x:ec2:Vpc with children aws VPC, awsx:x:ec2:Subnet (containing subnet, route table, association) and awsx:x:ec2:InternetGateway; in v2 it is awsx:ec2:Vpc with aws VPC parent of subnet vpc-isolated-1, route table, association and internet gateway; in v3 the aws VPC is the root with no awsx component.
Pulumi's state records both physical resources and the components that group them; each record has a Pulumi name called a URN, and managed resources also have a cloud-provider ID.
The legacy AWSX component wraps the subnet and internet gateway in separate components, while modern AWSX removes those wrappers and puts managed resources under different parents.
In the example, the Pulumi name of the subnet changes from `vpc-isolated-0` to `vpc-isolated-1` between legacy and modern AWSX.

Pulumi aliases handle changes to a resource's name, type, or parent when its saved state remains compatible, but do not by themselves remove component wrappers and transfer references to replacement resources.
A Pulumi docs page on resource aliases exists at /docs/iac/concepts/resources/options/aliases/.
A component registers a state migration callback through the `stateMigrations` resource option, together with an alias for the legacy component type.
The example's `migrateClassicVpc` function is defined in aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration/v2/migration.ts in pulumi/examples.
With a state migration, the alias lets Pulumi find the old component, and the callback receives the old component's saved state followed by the state of its children.

The state migration callback returns `newState` (the complete set of records replacing the old component and its children) and `successors` (a map from each disappearing old URN to the URN that takes its place).

In the example's first migration, an unexpected component type raises an error instead of guessing how to migrate, and the callback does nothing if state already uses modern AWSX or plain AWS resources.
The example's `rename` helper copies the saved record and changes its URN, type, and parent while preserving the AWS resource ID and other saved fields.

The `successors` entries let the Pulumi engine know that the old component wrapper and managed subnet point to the same new subnet record, and Pulumi uses these mappings to update dependencies and resource references elsewhere in the stack.
The VPC successor mapping keeps the security group's reference connected to the migrated VPC record, which retains the same AWS VPC ID.
The example's third version declares the VPC, subnet, route table, association, and internet gateway directly with `@pulumi/aws`.

The example's second migration (v3/migration.ts) removes the AWSX VPC component record and moves the managed VPC into its place, with both the old component and its VPC child mapping to the new VPC record, the VPC keeping its AWS ID.
The plain VPC registration keeps aliases for both previous component types and both migration callbacks.
Pulumi runs multiple state migration callbacks in order, passing each result to the next callback.

A stack still using legacy AWSX can upgrade directly to the plain AWS version, a stack already using modern AWSX skips the first migration, and after both migrations have run both callbacks return no result on later updates.
Keeping earlier migrations with the component means users can skip versions without editing stack state by hand.

After a state migration, Pulumi compares the new program with the migrated state and calls the provider for remaining changes; the example can still show in-place updates for provider defaults and tags.
Before each upgrade in the example, `pulumi preview` should show no creates, deletes, or replacements for the existing VPC, subnet, route table, association, internet gateway, and security group.
`pulumi preview` evaluates the state migration without saving it, and the update (`pulumi up`) saves the migrated state.

When users upgrade a component that registers a state migration and run Pulumi, Pulumi runs the migration automatically as part of the normal preview and update; users don't need to write the migration, attach the callback, or edit stack state.
For an internal component change that keeps the same inputs and outputs, users can keep their existing component calls when a state migration handles the saved-state changes.
Pulumi state migration callbacks (the state migrations resource option) run during previews and updates when prior state exists.
Pulumi state migration callbacks must be idempotent and must return no result when the state no longer needs migration.
Pulumi state migration callbacks rewrite state without performing provider operations.
A Pulumi component state migration callback is a pure function that transforms the saved state of a component and its children into the state expected by a new component version.
A Pulumi component state migration callback returns the updated state records and successor mappings.
In a Pulumi component state migration result, each successor mapping connects an old URN omitted from the result to the URN of the returned resource that takes its place.
If no migration is needed, a Pulumi component state migration callback returns no result.
The Pulumi state migrations option reference at /docs/iac/concepts/resources/options/statemigrations/#callback-api explains the callback API.
The state entries passed to a component state migration callback use the Pulumi checkpoint resource format, including fields such as urn, type, id, parent, provider, inputs, and outputs.
A state migration callback that returns no result can remain attached when using Pulumi update plans or targeted updates.
The restrictions on state-changing results of component state migrations (with update plans or targeted updates) do not require removing an already-applied migration.
